title: Power and its Three Faces

cards.h: Power is the core concept of politics
cards.b:
Some scholars call politics the study of power. Who has it? How is it used? Is it always bad? Where is it hidden? These questions run through all the units of Paper I.

The syllabus asks about "power, hegemony, ideology and legitimacy". This lesson covers power. The next two cover hegemony and ideology, then authority and legitimacy.

The standard way to teach power is through the three faces debate: Dahl, Bachrach and Baratz, and Lukes. Each critic said the earlier view missed something deeper. Add Foucault and Arendt for modern depth. Examiners ask both for the three-faces framework and for its application to Indian politics.

Basic definitions:

  • Max Weber, Economy and Society (1922): power is the chance of a person to carry out their will even against the resistance of others.
  • Robert Dahl (1957): A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something B would not otherwise do.
  • Hannah Arendt, On Violence (1970): power is the human ability to act in concert, so it needs a group. Violence is different. It is a tool that can destroy power.

Two ideas of power: power over (domination, A against B) and power to or with (the capacity to act together, as Arendt and Parsons thought).

Related terms: force (physical coercion), influence (persuasion), authority (power seen as rightful) and manipulation.

cards.h: The three faces at a glance
cards.b:
Each face goes deeper than the last. The first sees only the visible fight. The second sees the hidden fight. The third sees the fight that never starts because people have been shaped to accept things as they are.

Lukes's own 2005 second edition adds that the faces are not rivals. They are layers, and a full study of power looks at all three.

cards.h: First face: Dahl and the pluralists
cards.b:
Robert Dahl studied New Haven in Who Governs? (1961). His method: look at concrete decisions on real issues (urban renewal, schools, party nominations) and see whose preferences won. He found that no single elite won everywhere.

Assumptions of the first face:

  • Power can be observed in behaviour, in open conflict.
  • Interests are what people say they want (subjective interests).
  • If people do not take part, they are apathetic and content.

Critics objected that this view could not see the power that works behind the scenes. That led to the second face.

Peter Bachrach and Morton Baratz, "Two Faces of Power" (American Political Science Review, 1962), argued that power has a second face: agenda control. A can stop an issue from being raised at all, so B's grievances never reach the table.

They called this non-decision-making. It rests on a mobilisation of bias, a term from E.E. Schattschneider: institutions and rules that favour some issues over others. Methods include:

  • Threats and sanctions.
  • Rules of procedure and committee control.
  • Delay, and framing issues as "out of bounds".
  • Co-opting leaders.

Example: a company that hushes up pollution complaints, or a legislature that never takes up land reform.

Lukes's complaint: they still stayed with observable conflict. They also denied that any non-decision can happen without a visible grievance.

Steven Lukes, Power: A Radical View (1974, 2nd ed. 2005), added a third dimension: power to shape people's perceptions, preferences and beliefs. The most effective power stops conflict from arising by making people want what the powerful want.

"Is it not the supreme exercise of power to get another or others to have the desires you want them to have?"
Lukes, Power: A Radical View (1974)

This ties to Gramsci's hegemony and Marx's ideology. People may not see their real interests, which Lukes defined as what they would choose if they could do so freely and with full information.

John Gaventa, Power and Powerlessness (1980), tested this on Appalachian coal miners. Long inequality bred acceptance, which he saw as the third face at work.

Critics: how can an outsider judge someone's "real interests"? That risks elitism and paternalism.

cards.h: Foucault: power as relations, not possession
cards.b:
Michel Foucault (1926-84) changed the debate. In Discipline and Punish (1975) and The History of Sexuality, vol. 1 (1976), he argued:

  • Power is not something held by a ruler. It is everywhere, in relationships, institutions (prisons, schools, hospitals) and daily habits. It is "capillary".
  • Power is productive, not only repressive. It creates knowledge, categories and identities (the "criminal", the "patient").
  • Power/knowledge: knowledge and power are bound together. Who defines what counts as true holds power.
  • Discipline and surveillance: Bentham's Panopticon is the model. People who might be watched police themselves.
  • Biopower: states manage life itself, through health, census and population policy.

Where there is power there is resistance. Foucault does not offer a simple theory, but a way to see power.

cards.h: Other views: Marx, Mills, soft power
cards.b:
• Marxist: power flows from control of the means of production. The state serves the ruling class.
  • Elite theorists (Mills, 1956): power sits in a small circle. Mills added that institutional position gives power.
  • Michael Mann, The Sources of Social Power (1986): four sources, ideological, economic, military and political (IEMP).
  • Joseph Nye: hard power (coercion, payment) versus soft power (attraction through culture, values, policy), coined in Bound to Lead (1990) and developed in Soft Power (2004). Combining both is "smart power". This matters for Paper II.
  • Feminists highlight patriarchal power in family and body.

cards.h: Power in Indian society and politics
cards.b:
• Face 1: open contests, as in elections, legislative votes and court cases.
  • Face 2: issues kept off the agenda, e.g., manual scavenging or agricultural labour rights, often ignored in debates. Dominant castes and landlords controlled village councils. M.N. Srinivas's dominant caste (1959) explains local control.
  • Face 3: the internalised caste order. Ambedkar's "graded inequality" shows how hierarchy gets accepted. Gender norms also work in this way.
  • Foucault: surveillance and data, such as Aadhaar. The Supreme Court in Puttaswamy (2018) upheld Aadhaar with limits. Spyware claims over Pegasus (2021) raised the issue of state surveillance.
  • Gandhi offered a different view: real power rests in non-cooperation, because rulers need people's consent. Kautilya's danda (coercion) is the older state power.
  • Soft power: India's yoga, cinema and diaspora.

"Power has three faces." Elaborate.
Compare the pluralist and radical views of power.
Examine Foucault's contribution to the understanding of power.
Distinguish between power, authority and influence.

Structure: define power (Weber, Dahl). Present the three faces in order, each with author, work, method and critique. Add Foucault as a break from the 'power over' idea. Use Arendt to contrast power and violence. Illustrate with an Indian case such as caste or agenda control in village councils. End by saying the faces are layers, and each shows what the others miss.
